normalized.governing_thought: Do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027; sell fast delivery to grocers as software instead
executive_summary: Quick commerce is growing, but shoppers are not loyal enough to fill a store affordably – US quick-commerce sales grew 42% in 2025, to $5.1B – Filling nine stores would take about $27M of paid acquisition (p. 5–8)
No observed dark store makes money per order; only the founders' plan does – At benchmark medians a store loses about $6 on every order – Our own pop-up lost about $12.60 an order (p. 10–17)
The launch breaks the 12-month runway rule even if every plan assumption holds – The plan needs $9.5M; only $7.2M sits above the runway floor (p. 19–22)
Software is the better use of the cash, and its grocers want fast delivery – The grocer pipeline is worth 87% of today's ARR, for $0.8M a year of hires (p. 24–27)
Decline the launch, build fast delivery for grocers, reopen only if four signals turn – Grocer software alone meets both investor tests, and goes live in Q3 2027 (p. 29–33)

slides.title: Should Parcelbird launch its own quick-commerce service?
Key questions

claims.claim: Should Parcelbird launch Parcelbird Now, its own 15-minute grocery delivery service in three Midwest cities, in 2027, and reach profit within its $12.0M cash?
evidence: Sub-questions: 1 Will Midwest shoppers order often enough, at an acquisition cost we can carry, to fill nine dark stores? 2 Can a Parcelbird dark store reach contribution profit per order by month 18? 3 Does the launch fit within $12.0M of cash while keeping 12 months of runway? 4 Would the same cash do more in the software business? 5 What should the board decide in January, and what would make us reopen the question?
Decision maker: The board: two founders and two investors
Success criteria: A path to profitability within the current $12.0M cash, with no new round; At least 12 months of runway at all times; No harm to the growth of the software business
Timing: Board meeting, January 2027
Out of scope: A new funding round; Cities beyond the three; Buying an incumbent

slides.title: Demand will not fill the stores
Demand for quick commerce is growing, but in Columbus it is not loyal enough to fill a dark store affordably

claims.claim: The market is real and still growing fast, as the founders say
evidence: 41.7% growth in US quick-commerce grocery sales, 2025

claims.claim: Stated interest is high, but few pop-up customers kept ordering
evidence: 22% of pop-up customers still ordering in month three

claims.claim: Each customer is costly to win, and too few stay to fill a store
evidence: $38 acquisition cost per pop-up customer, paid social and first-order credits

claims.claim: Growth in the market does not settle the decision; whether each store can be filled at a cost we can carry does

slides.title: 1a: Quick commerce is a real growth market: US sales nearly tripled from 2022 to reach $5.1B in 2025

claims.claim: The founders' growth claim holds
evidence: US quick-commerce grocery sales (GMV), $B: 2022 1.8; 2023 2.6; 2024 3.6; 2025 5.1
41.7% growth in 2025, after 44% in 2023 and 38% in 2024

claims.claim: Every year: growth stayed close to the 40% a year the founders cite, while the market nearly tripled
Growth is not profit: both incumbents still lose money on every order (2d)
Midwest gap unproven: the pack has no data on who serves our three cities, so 'nobody owns the Midwest' is still a claim

slides.title: 1b: Interest overstates the habit: 44% say they would order weekly, yet only 22% of pop-up customers stayed

claims.claim: 44% of residents aged 25–39 say they would use it at least weekly
evidence: Survey of 1,500 Columbus residents
Stated intent, not behavior; the age group most likely to use the service; says nothing about price or promotions

claims.claim: 22% of pop-up customers still ordering in month three
evidence: Pop-up customer data, autumn 2026
Measured on 11,800 orders in six weeks
Promotions averaged 12% of AOV, so many came for the discount
Most acquired customers stop within three months

claims.claim: 3.1 orders a month by the customers who stayed
evidence: Less than once a week, even among loyal users
About 37 orders a year per retained customer
Too few to spread a $1.15M site cost

claims.claim: The survey and the pop-up cover different groups, so the two shares are not a like-for-like gap

slides.title: 1c: Filling nine stores to plan density would take about $27M of paid customer acquisition, more than twice our cash

claims.claim: Filling nine stores to plan density would take about $27M of paid customer acquisition
evidence: 17,661 retained customers a store needs: 1,800 orders a day at 3.1 orders a month each
÷ 22% of acquired customers still ordering in month three (pop-up)
× $38 acquisition cost per customer (pop-up)
× 9 dark stores in the founders' plan
= $27.5M of paid acquisition, against $12.0M in the bank

claims.claim: The estimate is generous to the plan
evidence: Customers still ordering in month three keep ordering 3.1 times a month, with no further churn
Every order comes from a paid customer; the pop-up data shows no organic acquisition
Even at the benchmark median of 900 orders a day, acquisition would cost about $13.7M
The founders' $9.5M budget covers capex, launch marketing and losses together

slides.title: 2a: At benchmark medians a dark store loses about $6 on every order, and rider cost is the largest drain

claims.claim: At benchmark medians a dark store loses about $6 on every order
evidence: Contribution per order, median of 14 sites, $, 2025: Goods margin 9.18; Delivery fee 1.99; Promotions -2.04; Picking, packing -3.1; Rider cost -7.396; Payment, packaging -1.3; Site fixed cost -3.501; Site contribution -6.167

claims.claim: Riders, not rent, sink the order
evidence: 62.7% of variable cost per order goes to riders

claims.claim: Before rent: the order already loses money before site fixed costs, so volume alone cannot fix it
Rider cost: at 2.4 orders an hour, each delivery carries more rider time than the delivery fee and promotions together
evidence: rider cost is $17.75 an hour ÷ 2.4 orders

claims.claim: Site fixed cost: $1.15M a year spread over 900 orders a day; it halves only if density doubles
evidence: Goods margin is AOV of $34 × 27%; site fixed cost is $1.15M ÷ (900 orders × 365 days)

slides.title: 2b: The founders' plan sits above the best site observed on all four operating levers at once

claims.claim: The founders' plan sits above the best site observed on all four operating levers at once
evidence: Benchmark median: AOV $34; promotions 6%; 2.4 orders per rider-hour; 900 orders per site a day
Columbus pop-up: $31; 12%; 2.1; 280 – Below the median on all four
Best observed site: $42; 6%; 3; 1,400 – Best AOV and best density came from different sites
Founders' plan: $45; 2%; 3.5; 1,800 – Above every site / Rider speed and density sit above the top of the benchmark range
Benchmark range: 1.9–3.0 orders per rider-hour and 400–1,400 orders per site a day. No site achieved the best AOV and the best density together

slides.title: 2b: The plan's $2 profit an order becomes a $6 loss at benchmark levels, and lower AOV alone erases it

claims.claim: The plan's $2 profit an order becomes a $6 loss at benchmark levels
evidence: Site contribution per order bridge, $: Founders' plan 2.019; Lower AOV -2.75; Higher promotions -1.36; Slower riders -2.324; Lower density -1.751; Benchmark median -6.167

claims.claim: Each lever alone takes most of the margin
evidence: 33.6% of the swing from plan to benchmark comes from a lower AOV

claims.claim: Lower AOV: $34 instead of $45 removes more than the whole plan margin on its own
Slower riders: 2.4 instead of 3.5 orders an hour; even the best site reached only 3.0
Promotions and density: each removes most of the plan margin; the pop-up ran promotions at 12% of AOV

slides.title: 2b: Even with the best AOV and rider speed combined, a store would need about 6,400 orders a day to break even

claims.claim: Even with the best AOV and rider speed combined, a store would need about 6,400 orders a day to break even
evidence: $3,151 site fixed cost a day ÷ $0.5 variable contribution per order at $42 AOV and 3.0 orders per rider-hour = 6,391 orders a day to break even
÷ 1,400 orders a day at the best site observed = 4.6x the best density any site has reached

claims.claim: Only the plan's own AOV and rider speed bring break-even within reach
evidence: With the plan's $45 AOV, 2% promotions and 3.5 orders an hour, break-even falls to about 836 orders a day
No site has combined the best AOV with the best density; this case is already generous
The benchmark range for orders per site a day runs from 400 to 1,400
Fixed cost per site stays at $1.15M a year at any volume

slides.title: 2c: Our software know-how did not carry over: the pop-up lost about $12.60 an order, twice the benchmark loss

claims.claim: Our test came in last
evidence: Site contribution per order, $: Founders' plan 2.019; Best observed site -1.757; Benchmark median -6.167; Columbus pop-up -12.572
2.04x the benchmark median loss per order

claims.claim: Columbus pop-up: missed the median on AOV, promotions and rider speed, at under a third of median density
Fair caveat: six weeks on a temporary site, and orders grew 18% a week, so density was still rising
Best observed: still loses money, even as a composite of two different sites
Pop-up fixed cost is the temporary site's annualised $650,000; at a permanent site's $1.15M the loss per order would be larger

slides.title: 2c: The pop-up lost money on demand and labor levers that our software alone does not set

claims.claim: Our software already runs the benchmark stores
evidence: 14 grocer sites on Parcelbird software
Inventory, picking and rider dispatch already run on our product
Their median store still loses money on each order (2a)

claims.claim: The pop-up's gaps were in demand
evidence: $31 pop-up AOV, against a $34 median
Promotions at 12% of AOV, twice the median
280 orders a day, under a third of the median
Small baskets and heavy discounts are shopper behavior, not software

claims.claim: Operating adds risks the software never carries
evidence: $38 to acquire each customer
Paid acquisition for every shopper we serve
Rider pay set by city rules in two of our three cities
A $1.15M fixed cost a year for every store

claims.claim: The founders' edge is real but sits in software; it does not transfer to running stores

slides.title: 2d: Scale has not fixed the model: both incumbents lose money on every order, and the regional player is shrinking

claims.claim: Each order loses money at both incumbents
evidence: Contribution per order, $, 2025: Zipcart (national) -1.9; QuickBasket (regional) -3.4

claims.claim: Losses run at a quarter to almost half of revenue
evidence: EBITDA margin, 2025: Zipcart -25.8%; QuickBasket -45.7%

slides.title: 3b: If the stores settle at benchmark medians, nine sites would lose about $18M a year, 1.5 times our cash
